claims.claim: Oliver characterises the chapter epigraphs of Assassin's Apprentice as excerpts from a public document written in a distant, scholarly voice.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022, pp. 45-66
claims.quote: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice

claims.claim: Oliver calls the chapter 13 epigraph describing Patience dry, impersonal and objective by contrast with the personal encounter that follows it.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter

claims.claim: Oliver notes that the lengthy chapter 13 epigraph about Patience contains no hint of the author's relationship to her.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: This lengthy excerpt contains no hint of the author

claims.claim: Oliver argues that as Assassin's Apprentice proceeds the epigraphs become increasingly infected.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: the epigraphs become increasingly infected

claims.claim: Oliver names the style that displaces scholarly discourse in the late epigraphs as that of imaginative fiction.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: by the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style

claims.claim: Oliver identifies chapter 22 of Assassin's Apprentice as an inexplicable narrative intrusion into the epigraphs.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: an inexplicable narrative intrusion into the epigraphs

claims.claim: Oliver identifies chapter 15's epigraph as the case where a poetic lyricism creeps into the narrator's epigraph style.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver concedes that the chapter epigraphs of Assassin's Apprentice have no separate attributions.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (141), Fall/Winter 2022
claims.quote: and have no separate attributions

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor define their object as epigraphs that refer to fictional sources in secondary worlds.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, 'Between World and Narrative: Fictional Epigraphs and Critical World-Building', Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 32.2 (2021)
claims.quote: epigraphs that refer to fictional sources in secondary worlds

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor give as the second function of world-intrinsic epigraphs the supply of details that extend, explain and familiarize the fictional world.
claims.source: Ekman and Taylor, 'Between World and Narrative', JFA 32.2 (2021)
claims.quote: give details that extend, explain, and familiarize the fictional world

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor give as the third function of world-intrinsic epigraphs the provision of perspectives with complementary or conflicting worldviews.
claims.source: Ekman and Taylor, 'Between World and Narrative', JFA 32.2 (2021)
claims.quote: provide perspectives with complementary or conflicting worldviews

claims.claim: Elliott's annotated Hobb bibliography summarises Oliver as noting the function of epigraphs as ethos-enforcing paratexts.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'The Fedwren Project: A Robin Hobb Annotated Bibliography', elliottrwi.com
claims.quote: he notes the function of epigraphs as ethos-enforcing paratexts

claims.claim: A reader-critic writing on Substack points to Ekman and Taylor's article as further reading on fictional epigraphs alongside Oliver's.
claims.source: Jeffrey David Outcalt, 'Extra Credit: Continued Reading for Hobb's Farseer trilogy', Substack
claims.quote: Between World and Narrative: Fictional Epigraphs and Critical World-Building

claims.claim: An uncredited content site asserts that each Farseer chapter begins with an in-world snippet ranging from historical treatises and herbalist journals to folklore and political propaganda.
claims.source: RPG StoryTellers (uncredited house byline), 'The Assassin's Canvas'
claims.quote: a snippet of in-world text ranging from historical treatises and herbalist journals
